title: How to Write a Subcontract Scope of Work That Prevents Change Orders on Lump Sum Jobs
summary: Learn how to write a subcontract scope of work that closes scope gaps before bid day. Practical guide with real $200K–$400K gap examples.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Lump sum subcontracts transfer risk to the sub, but only for work that is clearly named in the scope letter. Everything else is a dispute waiting to happen.
- The most expensive scope gaps follow a pattern: work between two trades, work the drawings show but no spec assigns, and work everyone assumes the other sub is covering.
- Specific document references, trade-tailored language, and a scope review checkpoint before issue are the three practices that separate tight buyout packages from ones that bleed change orders.
- Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) generates trade-specific scope packages from digital drawings, specs, and addenda in under 60 minutes, with every item traced to the exact page and section.


A lump sum subcontract is only as strong as the scope letter behind it. The price is fixed, but the scope is not fixed until it is written down in enough detail that no one can argue about it later.


Most change order fights on lump sum jobs do not start on site. They start in the bid package. A scope letter that says "as per plans and specs" hands the sub a blank check to claim anything that is not explicitly excluded. That phrase costs GCs hundreds of thousands of dollars per year.


This guide explains how to write subcontract scope of work letters that close those gaps before the sub even prices the job.


## Why Lump Sum Scope Letters Fail


On a lump sum job, the GC carries the risk of scope gaps. If work is on the drawings but not in anyone's scope letter, the GC absorbs it. That is the deal.


The problem is not that estimators are careless. The problem is that scope gaps are structural. They live in the space between trades, in the work the documents require without naming a responsible party, and in the coordination items both subs assumed the other was pricing.


Provision's[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , built from 200-plus GC interviews, found that the same gaps appear on nearly every project. A $300K lead-lined glass omission on a hospital imaging suite. A $400K roof cover board missing from a $50M project. A $200K wood flooring gap on a luxury condo. None of these were accidents. Each one was produced by a scope letter that described the category of work without naming the specific items inside it.


According to Arcadis, the average North American construction dispute in 2024 was worth $60.1 million. Errors and omissions in contract documents have repeatedly ranked as the top dispute cause in North America. That starts in pre-construction, not in the field.


## The Four Things a Strong Scope Letter Must Do


Before getting into the how, it helps to be clear on what a subcontract scope letter is actually trying to accomplish.


1. **Name the work clearly enough that the sub prices what you mean, not what they assume.**
2. **Assign every item from the drawings and specs to a specific trade.**
3. **Eliminate overlap so two subs do not both include the same line item.**
4. **Close the gap so nothing falls between two trades and gets priced by neither.**


That sounds straightforward. In practice, it requires a different approach than most GCs use at buyout.


## Start With the Drawings, Not Your Last Scope Template


The most common anti-pattern in scope writing is starting with a template from the last similar job and editing it to fit. It feels efficient. It is not.


Templates carry the assumptions of the last project. The sub list was different. The spec was different. The document set had different coverage gaps. When you copy the template, you copy the blind spots too.


The first habit of high-margin pre-construction teams is drawings-first scope writing. You read the full document set for the trade you are scoping, then you write what it requires. The template becomes a floor, not a ceiling. That distinction matters.


The[subcontract language chapter of the Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/subcontract-language-scope) captures this directly from a Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC: "It's descriptive: bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"


That level of specificity requires reading the drawings, not reading the last scope letter.


## How to Structure a Subcontract Scope Letter for a Lump Sum Job


### 1. Open With a Specific Document Reference, Not a General One


Every scope letter needs a list of the exact documents it covers: drawing set revision, spec date, addenda by number. "As per plans and specs" is not a document reference. It is a placeholder that invites disputes.


Name the revision. Name the addendum. If a later addendum changes something, the scope letter needs to reflect that change specifically. Addenda buried inside a general incorporation clause do not protect you.


### 2. Write Inclusions in Enough Detail to Be Priced


An inclusion that cannot be priced is not an inclusion. "Electrical work as required" does not tell the sub what to price. "Furnish and install all lighting fixtures per Schedule E-101, including lamps, drivers, and emergency battery packs" does.


Use the peanut-butter test from the Scope Gap Playbook. If your inclusion is so general that a sub could read it two ways, rewrite it. The goal is a scope letter so specific that there is only one way to price it.


Three things every inclusion line should name:


- The specific work (what is being done)
- The spec section or drawing reference (where it comes from)
- The scope boundary (where this sub's work ends and the next sub's starts)


### 3. Address Coordination Items Explicitly


Coordination items are the most common source of lump sum change orders. These are the jobs that sit between two trades: the embed the steel sub needs cast into the concrete sub's slab, the wall blocking the drywall sub does not include because the millwork sub assumes it is there, the flashing joint where the roofer stops and the siding sub starts.


Provision's[Scope Gap Index](https://provision.com/scope-gap-index) , covering 1,290 scope packages across 24 projects in Q3 2026, found that 74% of packages had at least one coordination flag. Anchors, embeds, and connections were the most flagged item in concrete, metals, and electrical packages. Sealants, flashing, and waterproofing joints were flagged in 82% of Division 07 packages.


These are not edge cases. They are the standard pattern. Every scope letter for a trade that interfaces with another trade needs to name the boundary explicitly.


### 4. Use Exclusions to Confirm Assignments, Not to Escape Them


Exclusions are not a way to avoid scoping work. They are a way to confirm that the work has been assigned somewhere else. An exclusion without a corresponding inclusion in another trade's scope is a gap.


Before you write an exclusion, ask: "Who is including this?" If you do not have a clear answer, you have a scope gap. Write it into the trade that owns it, not out of the trade that does not.


### 5. Assign Testing, Inspection, and Certification


Specs require tests. Inspections produce certificates. Somebody pays for them. On lump sum jobs, "somebody" defaults to the GC if no scope letter names the sub.


The Scope Gap Index found that testing, inspection, and certification was flagged in 86% of HVAC packages and 73% of conveying equipment packages. It was the most common flag in Division 01, Division 14, Division 23, Division 27, and Division 28.


Name the sub responsible for each required test and inspection. Reference the spec section. If the spec requires the test and your scope letter does not name who pays for it, you will pay for it.


### 6. Name Temporary Protection and Phasing Items


Temporary protection is flagged in 42% of all 1,290 scope packages in the Scope Gap Index. It is flagged in 85% of fire suppression packages and 94% of furnishings packages.


The pattern is consistent: somebody covers the finished floor while four other trades walk across it. The drawings rarely show who. The specs rarely name who. The scope letters rarely say who.


If you are issuing a scope to a sub whose work will be in place before other trades finish, name the protection requirement. Name who provides it. Name who removes it.


## The Anti-Patterns That Cause Lump Sum Disputes


The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) documents eight specific anti-patterns in scope writing. The ones that drive the most lump sum disputes are:


- **"As per plans and specs."** This is the most-cited anti-pattern. It transfers nothing to the sub because it names nothing specific.
- **Copy-paste from the last job.** The scope describes the last project, not this one. Gaps from the last project travel forward.
- **Junior estimators stuffing previous scopes verbatim.** No review, no tailoring, no document comparison. The scope goes out as a draft and comes back as a change order.
- **The five-minutes-before-bid review.** Scope letters sent with no review checkpoint are scope letters that have not been read as a set. Conflicts and gaps only appear when you read all the scopes together.
- **Trusting subs on a gentleman's agreement.** An Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC put it plainly: "We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope."


## The Pre-Issue Scope Review Checkpoint


One of the eight habits from the Scope Gap Playbook is the pre-issue scope review. Before any scope letters go to subs, read them together as a set.


The goal is to find three things:


1. Items included in two scopes (overlap that inflates your bid)
2. Items excluded from all scopes (gaps that become change orders)
3. Coordination items that cross trade lines without an owner


This checkpoint is not a final proofread. It is a gap audit. It requires reading each scope against the full document set, not just against itself.


At most GCs, this checkpoint is either skipped or rushed. That is where the $400K roof cover board gap happens. The item was on the drawings. It was in nobody's scope. Nobody read the scopes together before they went out.


## Trade-Specific Items That Belong in Every Scope Letter


Some scope items are so commonly missed that they warrant a checklist by trade. The[trade-specific scope gaps chapter of the Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) covers these in detail. The highest-frequency gaps by trade include:


Trade / Division Most Commonly Missed Items


Concrete (Div 03) Grouting base plates, anchor bolt setting, concrete pumping, slab assembly conflicts


Steel (Div 05) Embeds and anchor bolts, hoisting and rigging, miscellaneous metals not on structural drawings


MEP (Div 21-28) Generator field conditioning, motor starters, fire-rated louvres, lighting controls, the trench


Drywall (Div 09) Wall blocking, insulation, hollow metal door frames, gypcrete naming conflicts


Envelope (Div 07) Roof cover board, masonry-storefront flashings, interior versus exterior caulking, firestopping


Specialty Lead-lined glass (hospital), elevator exclusions, curtainwall mock-ups, mass-timber material protection


None of these items are obscure. Every one of them has generated a real change order on a real lump sum job. The $45K stone-depth mismatch between civil, structural, and architectural drawings on a single slab. The $10K glulam beam destroyed in a lay-down yard because no scope clause required material protection. These are documented examples from GC pre-construction teams, not hypothetical risks.

## Summary: What a Tight Lump Sum Scope Letter Looks Like


A scope letter that prevents change orders does six things:


1. Names the exact documents it covers, including addenda by number
2. Writes inclusions at enough detail to be priced without assumptions
3. Assigns every coordination item to a named trade
4. Uses exclusions to confirm assignments elsewhere, not to avoid them
5. Names who is responsible for testing, inspection, and certification by spec section
6. Names temporary protection requirements and who provides them


The GCs with the best margins on lump sum work do all six consistently, on every pursuit, on every trade. That consistency is the differentiator. It is not a talent advantage. It is a process advantage.


If your team is still using "as per plans and specs" as the workhorse clause in your scope letters, you are carrying risk that belongs in the sub's column. ## Frequently Asked Questions


### What should a subcontract scope of work include on a lump sum job?


A lump sum scope letter must name the exact documents it covers, write each inclusion in enough detail to be priced without assumptions, assign every coordination item to a specific trade, and name who is responsible for testing and temporary protection. Generic language like "as per plans and specs" transfers no risk to the sub and invites change orders.


### What causes the most lump sum subcontract disputes?


Errors and omissions in contract documents have repeatedly ranked as the top dispute cause in North America, according to Arcadis. At the scope letter level, the most common cause is coordination items that fall between two trades and get priced by neither. The average North American construction dispute in 2024 was worth $60.1 million.


### How do I close scope gaps between trades on a lump sum bid?


Provision's Scope Agent reviews the full digital document set across all trades together and flags coordination items where work sits between two scopes. It traces every item to the exact page and section. Doing this before packages go to subs lets estimators assign every item before the sub has a chance to claim it was not in their scope.


### What is a coordination flag in a scope letter?


A coordination flag marks work that sits between two trades, where neither sub's scope explicitly names it. Anchors and embeds, sealant joints at trade interfaces, and wall blocking are common examples. Provision's Scope Gap Index found that 74% of scope packages across 24 projects in Q3 2026 had at least one coordination flag.


### How long does it take to write a subcontract scope of work?


A thorough manual scope package takes roughly four days per project at the human estimator baseline. Provision's Scope Agent generates trade-specific scope packages from digital drawings, specs, and addenda in under 60 minutes, with every item cited to its source document. ProWest Constructors cut estimating time by 50% on their first project using Scope Agent.


### What is the most common mistake in lump sum scope writing?


The most common anti-pattern is writing "as per plans and specs" as the main scope description. It names no specific work, assigns no specific responsibility, and gives the sub room to claim anything not explicitly excluded. The second most common mistake is copying the scope letter from the last similar job without reading the current document set.


### Should exclusions or inclusions drive a subcontract scope letter?


Inclusions should drive the scope letter. Exclusions confirm that work has been assigned somewhere else. An exclusion without a corresponding inclusion in another trade's scope is a gap, not protection. Before writing an exclusion, every estimator should ask: "Who is including this?" If there is no clear answer, the item needs to be assigned before the packages go out.
